title: How LSD Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss LSD: its accidental discovery by Swiss chemist Albert Hoffman at Sandoz in 1943 and his bicycle ride on the first acid trip (Bicycle Day), early medical and CIA-era uses, the 1960s backlash and prohibition, myths (chromosome damage, acid flashbacks, fatal overdoses), how LSD is made and sold (blotter paper, the 1990s Supreme Court weight ruling), the trip experience and set and setting, brain-imaging research on the default mode network, cultural figures (Timothy Leary, Ken Kesey, Owsley Stanley), modern dangers like NBOMe, and a closing listener mail segment with John Hodgman on nostalgia.
topics: LSD brain scans default mode network

segments.title: Disclaimer, anniversary, and LSD myths
segments.summary: Josh gives a disclaimer and the hosts mark the show's anniversary and Bicycle Day. They introduce LSD's cultural reach and debunk myths: LSD is not absorbed through the skin, and it does not damage chromosomes or put holes in the brain. They cite Art Linkletter's daughter's suicide, the Doc Ellis no-hitter story, and the authorities' role in spreading scares.

segments.title: Hoffman's ergot research and discovery of LSD
segments.summary: Albert Hoffman at Sandoz worked with ergot, a rye fungus historically used in midwifery. At the Rockefeller Institute, researchers isolated lysergic acid, and Hoffman went on to synthesize LSD (LSD-25) after earlier compounds. Pharmacologists dismissed it, but Hoffman resynthesized it five years later.

segments.title: Hoffman's first acid trip and Bicycle Day
segments.summary: Hoffman accidentally absorbed some LSD and had the first acid trip. The next day he deliberately took about 250 micrograms, and rode his bicycle home, which gave rise to Bicycle Day. His doctor found him physically fine, and he later drank milk and described the experience in his journal.

segments.title: Animal experiments and the early marketing of Delysid
segments.summary: Hoffman dosed animals, including mice, cats, chimps, fish, and spiders. The hosts describe an Oklahoma researcher who dosed an elephant, which died. Sandoz marketed LSD as Delysid to psychiatrists, suggesting they take it themselves.

segments.title: Psychiatric use, psychedelic therapy, and the decline of research
segments.summary: LSD was used in psychiatry in the U.S. and Europe. European practice used low doses for patient disarming, while American psychedelic therapy used higher doses. Cary Grant's therapy story is discussed. LSD was outlawed in 1966, and research declined through the 1970s and 1980s.

segments.title: Making LSD: precursors and dangerous chemicals
segments.summary: The hosts describe the difficulty of making LSD: ergot culturing in the dark, extraction of alkaloids, and reagents like chloroform and anhydrous hydrazine, which are dangerous. Morning glory and Hawaiian baby woodrose seeds are alternative precursors. They emphasize they are not giving a recipe.

segments.title: Forms of LSD, blotter art, and sentencing
segments.summary: LSD appeared as microdots, window panes (gelatin), and blotter paper. A San Francisco acid museum displays blotter art. A Supreme Court ruling counted carrier paper toward the drug weight, leading to long sentences for small amounts.

segments.title: What an LSD trip is like
segments.summary: The hosts describe hallucinations as perceptual distortions the user recognizes as drug-induced, the role of set and setting, the typical 7 to 12 hour duration with a peak around halfway, and physical effects. They note risks for people predisposed to mental illness and the possibility of a lingering emotional hangover.

segments.title: Brain effects: thalamus theory and Imperial College brain scans
segments.summary: The hosts describe Andrew Sewell's 2011 thalamus gatekeeper theory and the newer Imperial College London brain-scan study. The study found LSD increases cross-network connectivity and weakens the default mode network, which the hosts link to ego dissolution and lasting positive outlook changes. They mention a small U.S. study with terminally ill cancer patients.

segments.title: Flashbacks, lethal dose, and deaths
segments.summary: Acid flashbacks are described as lacking evidence of LSD stored in the body, with hallucinogen persisting perception disorder mentioned as a possible explanation. LSD's lethal dose has never been established. A party overdose of seven milligrams led to hospitalization, but everyone recovered. Documented deaths are behavioral, not pharmacological.

segments.title: Addiction, tolerance, and scheduling
segments.summary: The hosts discuss LSD's low addiction potential because of rapid tolerance and unpredictable effects. They note LSD is a Schedule I drug despite not meeting the criteria. They describe a reported case of heavy users developing social problems.

segments.title: Cultural figures: Leary, Kesey, Owsley, and microdosing
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Timothy Leary and his 'turn on, tune in, drop out' phrase, Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters, and Owsley Stanley, who made LSD and was the Grateful Dead's sound man. They mention modern microdosing in San Francisco and dangerous designer drugs like NBOMe sold as acid.

segments.title: Listener mail: John Hodgman on nostalgia
segments.summary: John Hodgman joins by phone to respond to the hosts' earlier nostalgia episode. He argues nostalgia can be therapeutic in moderation but is a toxic delusion when it implies the past was better or can be regained, and links this to political movements. The conversation covers Star Wars, the prequels, and Hodgman's upcoming tour dates.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank Hodgman and give social media and website contact information.
